DraftKings Rejects Targeting Claims in Reply to Congressional Inquiry on VIP Programs

Published November 10, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

DraftKings has sent a six-page letter to Congress denying that it uses customer data to single out bettors who are likely to lose money, responding to an October 22 inquiry from Senator Richard Blumenthal and Representatives Paul Tonko and Valerie Foushee into the company's VIP and promotional practices. The reply, obtained and reported on by InGame/CDC Gaming, lays out a list of internal safeguards the company says are already in place around responsible gambling and high-value player marketing.

What prompted the inquiry

The lawmakers' questions followed a September investigation by The New York Times that alleged DraftKings had used machine-learning models to identify customers likeliest to gamble heavily and lose money, then directed promotions their way. DraftKings' letter disputes that characterization directly, describing its VIP and promotional programs as built to improve the customer experience rather than to extract money from vulnerable bettors.

The safeguards DraftKings pointed to

According to the letter, customers who are on self-exclusion or involuntary-exclusion lists receive no promotional offers at all, and promotions pause both during a customer's cooling-off period and for a period after they return to the platform. VIP hosts are instructed to refer any customer showing possible signs of problem gambling to the company's Responsible Engagement Team, with crisis-level cases prioritized, and hosts also conduct responsible-gambling reviews on a random sample of 10 customers every month. DraftKings said fewer than 1% of its customers sit in its top two VIP tiers, Diamond and Onyx. The company declined to disclose average wins or losses among its rewards members, calling that figure competitively sensitive, but pointed to adoption of its "My Stat Sheet" tool — used by nearly half of customers within a year of its March 2024 launch — as evidence of transparency around individual betting activity.

Why it matters for bettors

This exchange is one piece of a broader push for federal oversight of the legal sports betting industry, including the long-stalled SAFE Bet Act, and comes just ahead of a House hearing scheduled for November 11 on sports gambling's reach into college campuses. FanDuel faced a similar round of congressional questioning over its own VIP program earlier this year. None of this changes how any individual account is treated today, but it's worth bettors knowing that VIP and promotional targeting practices at major operators are now squarely on federal lawmakers' radar, with more scrutiny — and potentially more disclosure requirements — likely ahead. Our responsible gambling resources page has tools for anyone who wants to review or adjust their own account's limits regardless of how this inquiry proceeds.
